name: Reporting API (crash, CSP and deprecation reports)
plain: Sends the browser's own error, crash and policy violation reports to a site endpoint.
meaning: A site can learn when its page crashes, runs out of memory, hits a blocked resource or uses a deprecated feature on your device, and gets those reports even after the page closed. No prompt is shown.

access.persistence: Reports are queued and sent in the background, even after the tab is closed
access.revocation: Nothing to revoke (no permission is stored)
access.iframe: Per document and its Reporting-Endpoints header; cross-origin frames use their own policy
steps: Browser notices a violation, deprecation or crash
Browser sends a JSON report to the endpoint, possibly later
Page can also read some reports with ReportingObserver

limits.headline: Can get the browser's crash and error reports sent to the site
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens if the page crashes or breaks a site rule
can: Receive reports on crashes, out of memory stops and blocked content
Receive notes about old features your device used
Get the report even after you left the page
cannot: See anything you typed or saved
Know who you are by itself
See reports from pages it does not own

story.what_it_is: The browser sends its own crash, security policy and old feature warning reports to an address the site chooses.

marketing.name: Reporting API
marketing.pitch: Chrome says it lets sites receive reports about crashes, policy violations and deprecated features from real users.

marketing.name: Reporting API
marketing.pitch: Describes a standard way for browsers to send reports about problems to a site's chosen endpoint.

story.for_you: You never see these reports. When your browser blocks a bad script or a tab crashes, it quietly tells the site, so the team can fix the problem. Your browser may send some details with it.
story.for_makers: Teams use it to catch crashes and blocked content from real visitors, which a test lab would miss. It also helps teams roll out stronger security rules safely, in report only mode first.

use_cases.example: A bank turns on a strict content policy in report mode and learns which scripts it would block before it enforces.
A browser game studio gets crash reports from real players on rare phones.
A site learns that a feature it uses will be removed in the next browser, and plans a fix.
A retailer sees reports that a third party script is being blocked, and finds a broken checkout step.
A monitoring service collects reports across many sites and groups them by cause.
A publisher sees that an ad was blocked for breaking a rule and removes it.
A news site uses reports about intervention warnings to stop heavy ads that freeze the page.

technical_bounds: Report types vary: csp-violation, deprecation, intervention, crash, coep, coop, permissions-policy-violation, integrity-violation
Browsers batch reports and retry for a limited time; delivery is best effort and delayed
Reports cannot include page content, only the violation details and URL
Firefox supports the header from 130 and ReportingObserver from 149; Safari 16.4
The older Report-To header is removed from the spec in favour of Reporting-Endpoints

abuse: Collecting reports about the person's browser features and blocked extensions
